summary: Describes private SIP extensions between proxies so trusted elements owned by different providers in the PacketCable distributed call signaling architecture can swap trusted information about customers and calls. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5503.

eli5.summary: Phone companies that trust each other need to share facts about a call. This memo describes the extra notes they attach to call messages.

questions: how do phone companies bill calls across domains
how are phone calls traced for lawful intercept
subtitle: Private header extensions for trusted SIP proxies to exchange customer and billing information.

tldr.problem: Telephone service providers need to exchange customer-specific, billing, and regulatory information between their SIP proxies when calls cross domain boundaries, but standard SIP does not provide private mechanisms for this trusted information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3603 defines five private SIP header extensions that proxies can use only within closed administrative domains: P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID for call tracing, P-DCS-OSPS for operator services, P-DCS-Billing-Info for billing, and P-DCS-LAES and P-DCS-Redirect for lawful intercept.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 5503, which supersedes it with updated specifications for the PacketCable distributed call signaling architecture.

today: RFC 3603 is Informational and was superseded by RFC 5503, which provides updated specifications for the PacketCable distributed call signaling architecture. These extensions remain in use by telephone service providers in closed administrative domains to coordinate billing, routing, and lawful intercept information between trusted proxies.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines private Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) header extensions for use only between trusted elements in the PacketCable Distributed Call Signaling (DCS) Architecture. These extensions allow service providers to exchange trusted information about customers and their calls when handling residential telephone service at large scale.

The extensions solve a specific problem: when calls cross domain boundaries between different service providers, the proxies need to exchange information such as billing details, customer location (essential for emergency services), and regulatory information (such as lawful intercept requirements). Standard SIP headers do not provide mechanisms for this trusted, private information.
sections.eli5: When two phone companies handle a call together, they need to share secret information like who is paying and if the police want to listen. These headers let them pass that information safely between their trusted computers.

sections.title: The Trust Model and Scope
sections.content:
These extensions assume a trust boundary around systems owned and operated by a service provider. Inside the boundary live proxies, servers (voicemail, announcement, bridge), and billing systems. Outside the boundary lie customer premises equipment and third-party application servers.

The extensions are only applicable within closed administrative domains, or among federations of domains with pre-agreed policies. They are not suitable for general Internet use because they leak sensitive information about customer billing, location, and regulatory requirements. Use outside a trusted domain could expose this information and allow fraud or denial of service.
sections.eli5: These headers only work inside a company's private network, where everyone is trusted. If you send them on the open internet, bad people could steal information about customers or fake data about a call.

sections.title: The Five Private Header Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC defines five SIP header extensions, all prefixed with P-DCS- (Private Distributed Call Signaling):

P-DCS-Trace-Party-ID carries the calling party identity for customer-originated trace of harassing or obscene calls. A customer can request a trace, and this header ensures law enforcement receives the true identity of the caller even if the caller requested anonymity.

P-DCS-OSPS (Operator Services Position System) indicates special call processing: 'BLV' for busy line verification (an operator checks if a line is truly busy), 'EI' for emergency interrupt (an operator breaks into a call), and 'RING' for operator ringback. These are used only on calls from operator services systems.

P-DCS-Billing-Info carries billing and accounting information including a globally unique call identifier, a financial entity identifier, the charging account, calling and called party numbers, and routing numbers from local number portability lookups. This allows all billing systems in the network to track the same call and bill correctly.

P-DCS-LAES (Lawfully Authorized Electronic Surveillance) and P-DCS-Redirect support court-ordered wiretaps and call tracing. LAES specifies delivery addresses and encryption keys for surveillance data. Redirect tracks call forwards and redirects so intercepted copies follow the call's complete path.
sections.eli5: The first header tracks who called (for police). The second tells a phone to let an operator break in or check if it's really busy. The third header carries billing information. The fourth and fifth are for police wiretaps, with one saying where to send copies and the other tracking when calls get forwarded.

sections.title: How Proxies Use These Headers
sections.content:
The headers are added and removed by proxies at the boundaries of trusted domains. An originating proxy, which receives a request from an untrusted user agent, generates billing information and adds it to the initial INVITE. A terminating proxy, which sends the request to an untrusted endpoint, removes all private headers before sending the request outside the trust boundary.

Tandem proxies (those not originating or terminating the call) pass the headers through unchanged. This allows information to flow across multiple service providers' networks while staying within the federation of trusted domains.

For example, when a call connects from one provider's customer to another's, the originating provider's proxy adds billing information identifying the calling customer. The terminating provider's proxy checks for lawful intercept orders on its customer and may add surveillance information. Both proxies add their own billing identifiers to the same call so their back-office systems can match and bill correctly.
sections.eli5: When a call enters a company's network, the first proxy adds information. When it leaves, the proxy takes off the secret headers. Middle proxies just pass them along. This way the information stays secret inside the company's network but is removed before it goes to a customer's phone.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Billing, quality-of-service coordination, and surveillance information are highly sensitive. The RFC requires that proxies protect these headers from eavesdropping and tampering. IPsec or TLS MUST be used between proxies and between trusted user agents and proxies. Mutual authentication is required and may use pre-shared keys or trusted third-party certificate authorities.

Within each administrative domain or federation, security policies and procedures must define an interoperable set of options for IPsec or TLS. A minimum mandatory IPsec configuration is specified in the PacketCable Security Specification.
sections.eli5: Because this information is secret and valuable, connections between trusted computers must be encrypted and both sides must check that they are talking to the right computer. Password-style keys or digital certificates can be used to prove identity.
